query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy‐alloy nanoparticles, the onset and progression of melting are controlled by the preferential surface segregation of Cu atoms. Because Cu has a significantly lower melting point and lower surface energy compared with the other constituent elements, it migrates to the nanoparticle surface upon heating. This results in the formation of a thin, Cu‐rich, liquid‐like layer (premelting) at a temperature below the bulk melting point. Once this surface layer forms, it accelerates melting inward via enhanced atomic mobility and coalescence of adjacent liquid regions.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid, as‐synthesized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles with a near–homogeneous atomic distribution.
generation.intervention: Thermally ramp the nanoparticles in an inert atmosphere while performing controlled surface modifications (e.g., applying a passivating coating designed to inhibit Cu segregation) on a subset of samples.
generation.conditions: Identical nanoparticles (similar size distribution, e.g., 10–50 nm) subjected to gradual heating in a high‐purity inert gas (or high vacuum) environment; one set left unmodified while the comparison set has a surface treatment known to limit atomic segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: A Cu‐enriched liquid-like surface layer formed by preferential segregation.
generation.mechanism: Due to differences in atomic surface energies and melting points, Cu atoms diffuse to the surface during heating. The resulting Cu‐rich layer undergoes premelting at a lower temperature than the underlying high-melting-point matrix, thereby acting as a liquid “skin” that facilitates inward progression of melting via enhanced diffusion and local coalescence.
generation.predicted_outcome: Unmodified nanoparticles will exhibit an earlier appearance of a distinct, Cu‐rich, liquid layer at the surface—observable via in situ high-resolution microscopy or differential scanning calorimetry—compared with nanoparticles whose surfaces have been engineered to inhibit Cu segregation. This shall manifest as a lower onset temperature for detectable premelting and a more gradual melting progression from the surface inward relative to baseline.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with a uniform elemental distribution that, in the absence of Cu segregation, would melt more uniformly at a temperature close to the bulk melting point of the composite alloy.
generation.boundary: Nanoparticles with controlled size (e.g., 10–50 nm) processed and measured under inert or vacuum conditions with well‐defined heating rates; no significant oxidation or extrinsic impurity effects present.
generation.uncertainty: While Cu segregation is expected to dominate, the potential contributions of size‐dependent melting point depression and the roles of other elements (Fe, Ni, Cr, Co) in altering local energy landscapes are not fully excluded. Quantitative contributions of these competing effects remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles: one set in the as‐synthesized condition and another set coated with a thin, inert layer (e.g., silica) to inhibit surface diffusion. Heat both sets under identical inert-atmosphere conditions while monitoring surface composition and phase state in real time via in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC).
measurements: Onset temperature for appearance of a liquid-like (premelted) surface layer via in situ TEM imaging.
Elemental mapping (e.g., via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) to quantify surface Cu enrichment.
DSC measurements of melting endotherms to compare the melting onset temperatures of coated vs. uncoated nanoparticles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the unmodified and the surface-passivated nanoparticles exhibit the same onset temperature for surface premelting and show similar melting progression with no significant Cu enrichment at the surface, then the hypothesis that preferential Cu segregation is the governing mechanism would be falsified.
